## In-Class Tech {.figure-aside .golden}

::: {.caption}
Evidence reviewed in the [syllabus](../syllabus/): [Flanigan et al. (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09780-y); [Sana, Weston, & Cepeda (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2012.10.003).
:::

[TLDR: NO PHONES, NO LAPTOPS — TAKE NOTES ON PAPER]{.eyebrow}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.incremental}
::: {.dense-smaller}
- The purpose of our meeting time is to learn together
- So **by default, all class periods are free from cell phones, laptops, and tablets**
- I review the latest studies/evidence every year
- I looked at the evidence again in Summer 2026
- Sometimes we *will* use devices for an activity, usually at the end of class
- Using a phone/laptop has a **chain reaction** — it distracts the people around you too
- You will get a **worksheet** most sessions: guided notes, and a place to write down questions
- I know this is weird/unusual
- I will **revisit this policy** with you during the semester
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/lattice/question2.png" alt="A student in a lecture hall raising her hand over an open laptop, with classmates seated in the rows around her">
::::

:::::

## Benefits of Paper

::: {.caption}
Craik & Lockhart (1972); Mueller & Oppenheimer (2014); Morehead, Dunlosky, & Rawson (2019). In-class device evidence is in the [syllabus](../syllabus/).
:::


::: {.incremental}
::: {.dense-smaller}
- To keep a memory, you have to **encode** it
    - select, condense, connect it to what you already know
- Handwriting is too slow to transcribe
    - you are forced to decide **what matters**
    - deciding is learning!
    - deeper processing, more durable memory (Craik & Lockhart, 1972)
- Ask questions out loud - someone else might be wondering too
- A page has no notifications and no other tabs :-)
- One famous longhand study (Mueller & Oppenheimer, 2014) did not fully replicate (Morehead et al., 2019)
- But generally: distractions hurt learning
    - writing/processing/thinking helps
:::
:::

## Schedule Overview {.figure-aside .golden}

[Four units: wrangling, exploring, modeling, adventuring]{.eyebrow}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.dense-smaller}
- **Week 1** — intro; the lifecycle; asking questions
- **Weeks 2–3** — statistics review; Python, Polars, obtaining & wrangling data
- **Week 4** — exploratory analysis; descriptive statistics
- **Weeks 5–6** — visualization!!!!
- **Week 7** — hypothesis testing; estimation & sampling
- **Weeks 8–9** — regression; classification; trees; SVMs
- **Week 10** — clustering; PCA; model evaluation
- **Week 11** — recommendation systems; A/B testing, RCTs
- **Week 12** — network analysis;
- **Weeks 14–15** — presentations
:::

# Defining Data Science {.section-header}


## A Dictionary Definition

::: {.caption}
Definitions and etymology: Wiktionary, [*data*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/data), [*datum*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/datum) ([CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/))
:::

::: {.fragment .strike}
What is data?
:::

::: {.fragment}
What [are]{.key} data?
:::

::: {.fragment}
[data]{.term}: plural of [datum]{.term}, i.e. multiple datum, borrowed from Latin *data*, past participle of *dō*, "to give."
:::

::: {.fragment}
A [datum]{.term} is "a single recorded phenomenon, especially obtained by scientific work" literally *a thing that is given*.
:::



---


## What is Science?

::: {.caption}
Definitions and etymology: Wiktionary, [*science*](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/science) ([CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/))
:::

::: {.fragment}
[science]{.term} — from Latin *scientia*, "knowledge," from *scire*, "to know."
:::

::: {.fragment}
"The collective discipline of study or learning acquired through the [scientific method]{.key}"
:::

::: {.fragment}
"the sum of knowledge gained from such methods and discipline."
:::

::: {.fragment}
What does that make [data science]{.term}? Not "the science of data," moreso: [knowing, by way of things/data we are given]{.key}.
:::

::: {.fragment}
*Given* by whom? Chosen, measured, and recorded by a human being with situated knowledge (we'll come back to that).
:::


---


## What is Data Science?

[Data science]{.term} is an [interdisciplinary]{.key} field that studies and applies tools and techniques for [deriving useful insights from data]{.key}.

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="26%"}
::: {.dense-smaller style="text-align:center; margin-top:1.4em;"}
It uses techniques from [computer science]{.term} and [statistics]{.term}…
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
<img class="figure figure-sm" src="../assets/data-science-venn/data_science_venn_remix_v2.svg" alt="Venn diagram with three overlapping circles labeled Hacking Skills, Math and Statistics Knowledge, and Substantive Expertise. Their intersections are labeled Machine Learning, Traditional Research, and Danger Zone, with Data Science at the center.">
::::

:::: {.column width="26%"}
::: {.dense-smaller style="text-align:center; margin-top:1.4em;"}
…to find patterns and explain relationships using data from different [domains]{.term}.
:::
::::

:::::

::: {.caption}
Based on: Drew Conway, The Data Science Venn Diagram (2010)
:::

## A Terabyte in Phones {.figure-aside .golden}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.incremental}
::: {.dense}
- Fill up a 256 GB phone with photos — **4 full phones ≈ 1 TB**
- Every UIC student with a full phone: (**35,869** as of Fall 2025) ≈ **9,000 TB**
- Every Cook County resident with a full phone: (**5.2 million**) ≈ **1.3 million TB**
- Everyone in the US (**340 million**) ≈ **85 million TB**
    - Still less than the estimated 400 million terabytes created every day!
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/terabyte-scale/iphone-17-pro-max-cosmic-orange.jpg" alt="The back of a Cosmic Orange iPhone 17 Pro Max on a display stand at an Apple product launch, its three camera lenses in the raised bar across the top">

Populations: [Census Bureau 2024 estimates](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/popest.html); enrollment: [UIC Today](https://today.uic.edu/uic-enrollment-hits-all-time-best-mark/).

## A Terabyte in Streaming {.figure-aside .golden}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.incremental}
::: {.dense}
- **~30 hours of 4K video ≈ 1 TB**
- Stream 4K nonstop for **a week** ≈ **5.6 TB**
- Stream nonstop for **a month** ≈ **24 TB**
- Stream nonstop for **a year** ≈ **292 TB**
    - apparently the world creates that much 0.06 seconds
    - according to the 400 million terabytes per day estimate
- All **35,869** UIC students streaming 4K nonstop for a year ≈ **10.5 million TB**
    - Again less than the estimated 400 million terabytes created every day
:::
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/terabyte-scale/oppenheimer-format-guide.jpg" alt="The 'Oppenheimer' format guide: a two-column chart comparing film formats (IMAX 70mm, 70mm, 35mm) against digital ones (IMAX with laser, IMAX Xenon, DCP), each with its aspect ratio and resolution — IMAX 70mm is listed at a digital equivalent of about 18K pixels, DCP at 4096 x 1716">

::: {.caption}
*Oppenheimer* format guide, Universal Pictures / IMAX, via Rasmus Larsen, [FlatpanelsHD](https://www.flatpanelshd.com/news.php?subaction=showfull&id=1685963488) (2023); fair use. Capacities: [Kingston](https://www.kingston.com/en/memory-cards/storage-chart).

## What is Data Science? (A Hub of Fields) {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/week1-intro-data-science/role-of-data-science.svg" alt="Hub-and-spoke diagram: data science at the center linked to healthcare, transportation, climate science, public safety, and scientific research" class="r-stretch figure-plain">

---

## What is Data Science? (Yet Another Metaphor)

<img class="figure figure-lg" src="../assets/week1-intro-data-science/role-of-data-science-cta-remix-v2.svg" alt="A transit map of data science. Grey rail lines are labelled journalism, politics, sports, art, design transportation, general scientific research, education, public health, and climate science; the Orange Line, still in color, is labelled data science, runs up into the Loop, and ends in the southwest at &quot;your own project(s)&quot;.">

::: {.notes}
- Many fields "share the same track" (i.e. methods, tools, etc.)
- Data science makes up much of that shared track
- Data science can also go in a different direction
:::

---

## So what Do Data Scientists Do?

::: {.incremental}
1. **Ask good questions** — turn a vague goal into something measurable
2. **Obtain & clean the data** — collect, merge, and fix messy real-world data
3. **Explore & visualize** — search and discover patterns, outliers, and surprises
4. **Model & predict** — build something that explains and/or forecasts
5. **Communicate** — turn results into stories, decisions
:::

## Bohr's Quadrant: Curiosity {.figure-aside auto-animate=true}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column .dense}
::: {.incremental}
- What determines the stability of atoms?
- What is the molecular structure of caffeine?
- Does $P = NP$?
- "Pure basic research"
:::


::::

:::: {.column}
<img data-id="pq-grid" class="figure" src="../assets/pasteurs-quadrant/pasteurs-quadrant-complete.svg" alt="Pasteur's quadrant with all four cells shown and none highlighted">

::: {.caption}
Donald E. Stokes, *Pasteur's Quadrant: Basic Science and Technological Innovation* (Brookings, 1997).
:::
::::

:::::

---

## Edison's Quadrant: Uses, Applications {.figure-aside}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column .dense}
::: {.incremental}
- Which cold brew recipe do guests rate highest?
- Which version of the headline gets more clicks?
- What is the fastest route to CDRLC right now?
- **Less about "why."**
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/pasteurs-quadrant/pasteurs-quadrant-complete.svg" alt="Pasteur's quadrant with all four cells shown and none highlighted">

::: {.caption}
Donald E. Stokes, *Pasteur's Quadrant: Basic Science and Technological Innovation* (Brookings, 1997).
:::
::::

:::::

---

## Pasteur's Quadrant: Understanding and Use {.figure-aside}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column .dense}
::: {.incremental}
- Do noise machines help people sleep? Why or why not?
- How does the running plan influence people's performance?
- Which bus stops have the longest wait times?
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Knowledge you can act on *and* learn from.**
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/pasteurs-quadrant/pasteurs-quadrant-complete.svg" alt="Pasteur's quadrant with all four cells shown and none highlighted">

::: {.caption}
Donald E. Stokes, *Pasteur's Quadrant: Basic Science and Technological Innovation* (Brookings, 1997).
:::
::::

:::::

---

## More Example Questions

:::: {.dense}
::: {.incremental}
- Do guests like the new cold brew recipe?
- Is the running plan helping people run faster?
- Do people sleep better with noise machines?
- Does surveillance improve safety?
- Did the advertising campaign make a difference?
- 
- **No real, curious human wants just "yes" or "no."**
- Data scientists can *explain* answers in detail.
- (See mini-book, [Chapter 1: Working Toward Wisdom](../ethics-in-data-science/book/01-working-toward-wisdom.html)).
:::
::::

## Is the Pyramid Upside Down? {.figure-aside}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.incremental}
- Tuomi (1999): "data emerges only after we have information...  information emerges only after we already have knowledge"
- You need knowledge to decide what is even worth measuring
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/pyramid/upside-down-pyramid-bratislava.jpg" alt="The Slovak Radio Building in Bratislava, an inverted pyramid resting on its point">

::: {.caption}

:::
::::

:::::

---

## So, Is the Pyramid Upside Down? {.figure-aside}

::::: {.columns}

:::: {.column}
::: {.incremental}
- Does wisdom sit at the top of the pyramid?
- Or does wisdom hold up the whole thing?
- What else could be messing in this metaphor?
:::
::::

:::: {.column}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/pyramid/upside-down-pyramid-bratislava.jpg" alt="The Slovak Radio Building in Bratislava, an inverted pyramid resting on its point">

::: {.caption}
Slovak Radio Building, Bratislava. Thomas Ledl, [*Upside down Pyramid, Bratislava 02*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Upside_down_Pyramid,_Bratislava_02.jpg), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/).
:::
::::

:::::

## Provenance {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.dense-smaller}
- Analogy: data scientists can explain *why* the figure was not a perfect triangle
- and are willing to say why it *is*, in some sense, a triangle
- understand how "subpixels of data" become "images of information"
- "All models are wrong" (Box)
	- All **data** are wrong too!
	- Or at least incomplete
:::

<img class="figure figure-sm" src="../assets/pyramid/06-dikw-pyramid-full.svg" alt="The full DIKW pyramid with all four layers labeled: data, information, knowledge, and wisdom">

::: {.caption}
See [Chapter 1: Working Toward Wisdom](../ethics-in-data-science/book/01-working-toward-wisdom.html).
:::

## Random Roll Call {.iframe-slide}

<div class="random-draw" data-num="12" data-min="1" data-max="62">
<div class="random-draw-frame">
<div class="random-draw-numbers" role="status" aria-live="polite" data-placeholder="Press “Draw” for 12 random numbers between 1 and 62."></div>
</div>
<p class="random-draw-controls"><button type="button" class="random-draw-button">Draw</button> <span class="random-draw-status"></span></p>
</div>

<style>
.random-draw { display: flex; flex-direction: column; flex: 1; min-height: 0; }
.random-draw-frame { flex: 1; min-height: 0; display: flex; justify-content: center; }
.random-draw-numbers { height: 100%; aspect-ratio: 1.618 / 1; max-width: 100%; border: 1px solid #999; display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); grid-template-rows: repeat(3, 1fr); place-items: center; }
.random-draw-numbers .random-draw-number { font-size: 3rem; font-weight: 700; line-height: 1; }
.random-draw-numbers .random-draw-placeholder { grid-column: 1 / -1; grid-row: 1 / -1; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4rem; color: #555; padding: 0 1.5em; }
.random-draw-controls { flex: none; margin: 12px 0 0; }
.random-draw-button { font: inherit; font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; padding: 0.3em 1.2em; border: none; border-radius: 3px; background: #f9461c; color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
.random-draw-button:hover:not(:disabled) { background: #e03c14; }
.random-draw-button:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: default; }
.random-draw-status { font-size: 1rem; color: #555; margin-left: 0.75em; }
</style>

<script>
(() => {
  const API = "https://www.random.org/integers/";
  function setup(root) {
    if (root.dataset.wired) return;
    root.dataset.wired = "1";
    const out = root.querySelector(".random-draw-numbers");
    const button = root.querySelector(".random-draw-button");
    const status = root.querySelector(".random-draw-status");
    const num = root.dataset.num, min = root.dataset.min, max = root.dataset.max;
    const url = API + "?num=" + num + "&min=" + min + "&max=" + max + "&col=1&base=10&format=plain&rnd=new";
    function placeholder(text) {
      out.innerHTML = "";
      const p = document.createElement("div");
      p.className = "random-draw-placeholder";
      p.textContent = text;
      out.appendChild(p);
    }
    function render(numbers) {
      out.innerHTML = "";
      numbers.forEach(function (n) {
        const cell = document.createElement("div");
        cell.className = "random-draw-number";
        cell.textContent = n;
        out.appendChild(cell);
      });
    }
    function draw() {
      button.disabled = true;
      status.textContent = "drawing from random.org…";
      fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" })
        .then(function (r) { if (!r.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + r.status); return r.text(); })
        .then(function (text) {
          const numbers = text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
          if (!numbers.length) throw new Error("empty response");
          render(numbers);
          status.textContent = "true random numbers from random.org";
        })
        .catch(function (err) {
          placeholder("Could not reach random.org (" + err.message + "). Open the draw in a new tab instead.");
          status.textContent = "";
        })
        .then(function () { button.disabled = false; });
    }
    button.addEventListener("click", draw);
    placeholder(out.dataset.placeholder);
  }
  function init() {
    document.querySelectorAll(".random-draw").forEach(setup);
  }
  if (document.readyState === "loading") {
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", init);
  } else {
    init();
  }
})();
</script>

# More about Questions {.section-header}


## Questions in the Data Science Lifecycle {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/lifecycle/ds-lifecycle-v1.svg" alt="The data science lifecycle with the 'ask a question' stage highlighted; obtain data, understand the data, understand the world, and reports, decisions, solutions are shown unhighlighted.">

## Susanne Langer {.quote-slide}

> The way a question is asked limits and disposes the ways in which any answer to it — right or wrong — may be given.

::: {.attribution}
Susanne Langer
:::

::: {.quote-source}
*Philosophy in a New Key* (1942).
:::

---

## Which Question is Better?
::: {.caption}
Examples from Booth et al., *The Craft of Research* (2024).
:::

::: {.incremental}
- "Are there ultimate particles?"
- "Was Abraham Lincoln's right thumb longer than his nose?"
- Both are concrete and answerable!
- Today we will develop vocabulary to describe the differences
:::

# Basic Types of Questions {.section-header}


## Basic Types of Questions {.split}

::: {.split-content .narrow-aside .fill-height}

::: {.dense}

::: {.caption}
Taxonomy from the *Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy* entry on questions.
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **"Whether"** — a finite set of direct answers (yes/no, multiple choice)
- **"Which"** — seeks a person, thing, or value; possibly infinite answers
- **"Why"** — asks for an explanation, not just a fact
- **Indirect ("embedded")** — implied by a larger statement ("Bob knows who spoke to Mary")
:::

:::

![](../assets/lattice/question2.png){.figure alt="A student in a lecture hall raising her hand, with classmates seated in the rows around her"}

:::



---

## What About "How" Questions?

::: {.incremental}
- Paraphrase test: if "how" can be reworded as "**in what way**," it is explanation-seeking (a "why" question)
- Otherwise it asks for a value (a "which" question)
- "How far is it to Cleveland?" (a distance)
- "How does screen time influence mental health?" (an explanation)
:::

---


## Cross's Seven "Ways"

::: {.caption}
Charles B. Cross, ["Explanation and the Theory of Questions"](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00385722), *Erkenntnis* 34(2), 1991, pp. 248–249.
:::

:::: {.dense}
::: {.incremental}
- **By what road** — the route taken ("How did you get here?")
- **In what manner** — the style of the doing ("How did you behave at the party?")
- **By what argument** — the reasoning offered ("How will you justify this?")
- **By what method** — the established procedure ("How do you perform an appendectomy?")
- **By what means** — the resource or instrument used ("How did you get that money?")
- **In what respect** — the dimension of comparison ("How do these differ?")
- **By what process** — the mechanism unfolding over time ("How do DNA molecules replicate?")
:::
::::

---


# Common Pitfalls in Questions {.section-header}


## Carl Sagan {.quote-slide}

> There are naïve questions, tedious questions, ill-phrased questions, questions put after inadequate self-criticism. But every question is a cry to understand the world.

::: {.attribution}
Carl Sagan
:::

::: {.quote-source}
*The Demon-Haunted World: Science as a Candle in the Dark* (1995).
:::

---

## Common Pitfalls {.split}

::: {.split-content .narrow-aside}

::: {}

::: {.incremental}
- Naïve questions
- Tedious questions
- ill-phrased questions
- Leading questions
- Settled, speculative, or dead-end
- Invasive questions
- "Gotcha" questions
:::

:::

![](../assets/lattice/question2.png){.figure alt="A student in a lecture hall raising her hand, with classmates seated in the rows around her"}

:::

---

## Naïve Questions

::: {.incremental}
- Naïve about a particular context or setting
- Can also reveal assumptions "experts" have stopped considering
- e.g. "Was Michael Jordan good at basketball?"
- e.g. "Which NBA players are the best scorers?"
	- points per game vs. efficiency, possession context, etc.
:::



---

## Tedious Questions

::: {.incremental}
- Effort to answer is disproportionate to the value of the answer
- Measurable details are not always meaningful
- "How many times did each council member say the word 'budget'?"
    - (e.g. but ignoring how they actually voted)
:::

---


## ill-Phrased Questions

::: {.incremental}
- Terms, scope, or possible answers are unclear
- "Are students doing better this year?"
	- which students, compared with when, by what metric?
- "Is our museum's collection diverse?"
	- diverse in who/what/when, counted how?
- "Is news coverage biased?"
	- in story selection, sourcing, or word choice?
:::

---

## Leading Questions

::: {.incremental}
- Implies a preferred answer
- "How much did the tutoring program raise test scores?"
- "Everything tasting good over here?"
- Other examples of leading questions?
:::

---



## Settled, Speculative, and Dead-End Questions

::: {.incremental}
- **Settled** — already answered "well enough"
	- although replication studies can change this!
- **Speculative** — no evidence could realistically settle it
	- ("what if I-90 had never been built?")
- **Dead end** — answerable and precise, but nothing follows
	- ("how many bus stops face north?")
:::

---

## Invasive Questions

:::: {.dense}
::: {.incremental}
- All questions ask for information
- But information sensitivity can exceed the context
    - "Contextual integrity"
- E.g. Asking your weight at a job interview vs. at the DMV
- Can become coercive, e.g. if answers required for grades, jobs, housing, healthcare
- Ask for the **least sensitive** data that can address the question
    - More on this when we get to obtaining data, privacy
:::
::::

---

## "Gotcha" Questions {.split}

::: {.split-content .narrow-aside}

::: {}

::: {.incremental}
- Asked to call someone out, not to learn/explore
- The asker already knows the answer they want
- "What's the sample size for that?"
- sometimes a matter of how it's said
- Usually best saved for politicians / laywers
:::

:::

::: {.captioned-figure}
![](../assets/lattice/question2.png){.figure alt="A student in a lecture hall raising her hand, with classmates seated in the rows around her"}

::: {.caption}
"If Thanos was so worried about overpopulation, why didn't he use the magic glove to make more food?"
:::
:::

:::

---


# Temporality and More {.section-header}


## Presuppositions

::: {.incremental}
- A **presupposition** is a background claim that must be true for the question to have a meaningful answer
- "Who was the Roman emperor in 2020?"
- Presupposes an active Roman Empire
- Try to name your presuppositions!
:::

---

## Contrast Classes

:::: {.dense}
::: {.incremental}
- Explanatory questions often presuppose a set of alternatives
	- "compared to **what**?"
- "How do DNA molecules (vs. benzene and hexane) replicate?"
	- only one replicates -> no contrast class
- "How do reptiles (vs. mammals and birds) reproduce?"
	- every member reproduces -> contrast classes!
- A different "contrast class" can imply a different study design
:::
::::

---

## Temporality in Questions

::: {.incremental}
- Past/Present/Future
- **Counterfactual** — what would have happened?
- **Descriptive** — what is happening now?
- **Predictive** — what might happen in the future?
:::

---



## The Question can be the Hard Part {.quote-slide}

> In my opinion, the social sciences are the hard sciences.

::: {.attribution}
Michael Shermer
:::

::: {.quote-source}
*The Mind of the Market* (2008).
:::

---

::: {}

- Write down as many questions as come to mind
- Anything you are curious about
- Ideally, questions that could be addressed with data
